sources.title: Republic of Botswana: World Bank Group Country Climate and Development Report
sources.temporal_coverage: Country climate-development diagnostic published in 2025; combines historical observations and referenced studies with current-risk overlays and scenarios extending to 2050.

sources.title: National Drought Plan: Republic of Botswana
sources.organization: Republic of Botswana, prepared by Nnyaladzi Batisani under the UNCCD Drought Initiative
sources.temporal_coverage: Historical droughts through the 2020 plan; includes a 2015 vulnerability assessment, RCP4.5/8.5 projections and proposed 2020-2023 actions.
sources.methodology: National drought-risk synthesis and proposed sectoral governance actions.
sources.limitations: Uses a 2015 risk assessment; recommendations are not evaluated implementation or current status.

sources.title: Makgadikgadi Framework Management Plan 2010, Volume 2, Chapter 5: Wildlife Resources and Human Wildlife Conflict
sources.organization: Department of Environmental Affairs, Government of Botswana, with the Centre for Applied Research
sources.temporal_coverage: Assesses historical and current-at-the-time wildlife and human-wildlife conflict patterns, with focus groups in April-May 2010.
sources.methodology: Combines DWNP Problem Animal Control records, multi-year aerial counts, spatial mapping and 18-22-person focus groups in four villages.
sources.limitations: The report warns aerial counts vary in coverage and may substantially undercount; focus-group findings are historical and site-specific.

sources.title: Human-wildlife conflict a growing challenge
sources.organization: Botswana Daily News / Botswana Press Agency, reporting an Acting Director of the Department of Wildlife and National Parks briefing
sources.temporal_coverage: Reports a February 2025 briefing, including national wildlife-conflict figures for 2022-2024.
sources.methodology: Government newspaper account of an Acting DWNP Director's Ntlo ya Dikgosi briefing; incident figures are attributed to the speaker.
sources.limitations: Not an independent incident dataset; the account provides national statements without named hotspots.

sources.title: Gender and Equity Considerations for Building Climate Resilience: Lessons from Rural and Periurban Botswana
sources.organization: Kutlwano Makwatse, Leatile Modie, Morati Mpalo and Caitlin Blaser Mapitsa; Sustainability (MDPI)
sources.temporal_coverage: Household baseline research in Xhumaga and Ramotswa, reported in 2022; exact fieldwork dates are not stated.
sources.methodology: Participant-coded household narratives and survey with 141 residents in Xhumaga and Ramotswa, followed by community feedback meetings.
sources.limitations: Quasi-random qualitative sample, not statistically representative; fieldwork dates are unstated and participant data are restricted on ethical grounds.

claims.locator: One-based PDF p. 38, smallholder and rainfall-shock vulnerability discussion
claims.paraphrase: The CCDR reports poorer villages face more excessive or deficient rainfall; poorer smallholders are highly exposed to food insecurity and unstable livelihoods and lack resources to adapt.

claims.locator: One-based PDF p. 39, Figure 23 drought and flood vulnerability overlay
claims.paraphrase: Highest drought-vulnerability pockets are Southern District, Kgalagadi and western Ghanzi; Ngamiland Delta subdistrict and Francistown combine high flood risk with many poor households.
claims.limitations: Staff overlay, not an event forecast.

claims.locator: One-based PDF p. 38, Ngamiland East smallholder adaptation discussion
claims.paraphrase: In Ngamiland East, smallholders use hybrid seeds, changed planting and water harvesting; access to credit remains a barrier to investment.
claims.limitations: The CCDR cites an earlier study, not a new field survey.

claims.locator: One-based PDF pp. 17 and 38-39, social exclusion and climate vulnerability discussion
claims.paraphrase: Kalahari communal pastoralists are disproportionately affected by land privatization; Ngamiland, Chobe and Central combine high climate impacts with social exclusion, whose reported drivers include process-legitimacy and social-cohesion challenges.
claims.limitations: Co-location does not establish that climate impacts cause social conflict.

claims.locator: One-based PDF p. 39, gendered climate exposure and adaptation discussion
claims.paraphrase: The CCDR says women's water-collection and natural-resource roles heighten climate exposure; Bogakhwe knowledge, drought-tolerant crops and livelihood diversification support adaptation, while female-headed households in Kweneng show resilience and women report less institutional confidence.
claims.limitations: Synthesizes cited studies from different years.

claims.locator: One-based PDF pp. 56-57, 2015 drought-risk assessment and administrative areas
claims.paraphrase: The plan's 2015 assessment found over 50% precipitation shortfalls in parts of Ngamiland, Ghanzi and Kgalagadi; other high-risk areas had 25-50% deficits.
claims.limitations: Historical mapping, not a current risk ranking.

claims.locator: One-based PDF pp. 53-55, climate projections and agricultural impacts
claims.paraphrase: Under RCP4.5/8.5, suitability decreases for finger millet, beans and maize but increases for sorghum; aridity threatens livestock and western grazing.

claims.locator: One-based PDF pp. 59-62, drought monitoring and early-warning diagnosis
claims.paraphrase: In 2020 the plan described drought monitoring and impact assessment as reactive; it noted sparse hydrometeorological stations and missing data, and proposed community-engaged early warning.
claims.limitations: Dated institutional baseline; later status was not checked.

claims.locator: One-based PDF p. 60, drought declaration and relief options
claims.paraphrase: The plan describes presidential drought declarations after interministerial assessment and lists possible public works, under-five clinic feeding and farm-subsidy responses.
claims.limitations: Plan options, not proof of delivery or outcome.

claims.locator: One-based PDF p. 65, drought mitigation and integrated water management
claims.paraphrase: Proposed drought measures include integrated water management to mitigate upstream-downstream water-user conflicts and coordinate users, communities and sectors.
claims.limitations: Policy intention; violence is not specified.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The plan explicitly places water-user conflict mitigation within drought-risk management.

claims.locator: Printed p. 83 (one-based PDF p. 90), drought and water-resource conflict in Makgadikgadi
claims.paraphrase: The plan says drought concentrates people and wildlife around remaining water points and identifies the Boteti River as an existing Makgadikgadi human-wildlife-conflict focus.
institutions: Department of Wildlife and National Parks
claims.limitations: Historical plan analysis; no current incidence estimate.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: It explicitly links drought-driven shared-water pressure to human-wildlife conflict along the Boteti.

claims.locator: Printed p. 83 (one-based PDF p. 90), future water-resource and HWC risk
claims.paraphrase: The authors warn climate change could further constrain surface water and grazing, increasing human-wildlife conflict across Makgadikgadi and much of Botswana.
claims.scenario: Qualitative climate-change risk; no emissions scenario or calendar horizon is stated.
institutions: Department of Wildlife and National Parks
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The report expects climate-related resource constraints to increase human-wildlife conflict.

claims.locator: Printed pp. 106-107 (one-based PDF pp. 113-114), focus-group reports on compensation
claims.paraphrase: At Gweta, Phuduhudu, Rakops and Mmatshumo, focus groups said low or late compensation left farmers bitter toward wildlife and government; the plan judged direct compensation ineffective as appeasement.
institutions: Department of Wildlife and National Parks
claims.limitations: Four village discussions in 2010; not current opinion or a representative survey.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The report explicitly connects inadequate compensation to antagonism toward government and wildlife.

claims.locator: Article paragraphs 2-3, Acting DWNP Director's February 2025 briefing
claims.paraphrase: The Acting DWNP Director said climate-change effects exacerbate human-wildlife conflict; agricultural land demand and settlement encroachment into wildlife habitat were additional drivers.
institutions: Department of Wildlife and National Parks
claims.limitations: Official briefing statement, not an incident-level causal analysis.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: The official explicitly attributed part of intensified human-wildlife conflict to climate-change effects, alongside land and settlement pressures.

claims.locator: Article paragraphs 4-5, reported livelihood impacts, retaliation and casualty figures
claims.paraphrase: The official said crop and livestock losses, injuries and deaths damage livelihoods and can trigger resentment and retaliatory animal killing; he reported eight deaths each year in 2022-2024 and 8, 17 and 14 injuries.
institutions: Department of Wildlife and National Parks
claims.limitations: Speaker-reported counts; the article notes possible underreporting.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: He linked human-wildlife-conflict losses and casualties to resentment and sometimes retaliatory wildlife killings.

claims.locator: Printed pp. 4-5 (one-based PDF pp. 4-5), Xhumaga drought, shared water and HWC conditions
claims.paraphrase: In Xhumaga beside Makgadikgadi National Park, drought dried the seasonal river; a broken boundary fence and failed backup borehole left people and elephants sharing water, amid crop damage and reported trampling.
institutions: Department of Wildlife and National Parks
claims.limitations: Site observations, not a trend or incidence estimate.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Authors link drought, shared water and failed barriers to rising human-wildlife-conflict tensions.

claims.locator: Printed p. 5 (one-based PDF p. 5), gendered exposure and household adaptive capital in Xhumaga
claims.paraphrase: Xhumaga women responsible for household water collection were especially exposed to human-wildlife conflict shifts; households had little capital for climate-adaptive planning.
claims.limitations: Site-specific finding; authors note limited local gender data.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Authors explicitly connect women's water-collection role to climate-compounded human-wildlife-conflict vulnerability.

claims.locator: Printed pp. 5-6 (one-based PDF pp. 5-6), Ramotswa-Xhumaga comparison
claims.paraphrase: Ramotswa households had more formal employment and livelihood diversity, and greater capacity to withstand drought and flood shocks than Xhumaga, but faced dry taps, billing, maintenance and outage barriers.
claims.limitations: Two-site comparison; not a population estimate.

search_audit.query: Botswana subnational climate vulnerability poorer villages drought flood poverty named district reports Ngamiland Kgalagadi Ghanzi Francistown
search_audit.outcome: Read the 2025 CCDR, National Drought Plan and a two-site Xhumaga-Ramotswa study; found named drought/flood and rural-livelihood differences, with dates and representativeness limits recorded.

search_audit.query: Botswana climate change drought human-wildlife conflict HWC Boteti Xhumaga official primary report
search_audit.outcome: Inspected the Makgadikgadi plan, 2022 Xhumaga-Ramotswa study and 2025 official briefing; these explicitly connect drought or climate effects to human-wildlife conflict. No inspected report establishes climate-driven armed or intercommunal violence.

search_audit.query: Botswana violence conflict disrupts climate adaptation drought response reverse pathway conflict peace security report
search_audit.outcome: No inspected source documents armed conflict or intercommunal violence interrupting adaptation or disaster response. Local sources report HWC livelihood loss and compensation-related antagonism; a 2026 Boro study's full text was blocked and its abstract was not used.

search_audit.query: Botswana district drought early warning capacity response resilience social protection climate adaptation government
search_audit.outcome: Reviewed the drought plan's monitoring/response arrangements, the CCDR's mapped coping differences and the two-site study's household adaptation capacities; implementation status is dated or unevenly documented.

gaps: No inspected primary source establishes climate-driven armed violence or intercommunal violence in Botswana, or armed conflict disrupting adaptation delivery. The best-supported FCV pathway is drought/climate stress interacting with human-wildlife conflict, livelihood losses and retaliatory risk; these are not equated with armed conflict.
The 2010 Makgadikgadi plan and 2022 Xhumaga-Ramotswa study are location-specific and dated. The 2025 official HWC briefing is national and not locally disaggregated.
The 2020 National Drought Plan cites a 2015 risk map and proposed actions for 2020-2023; later plan implementation and current monitoring capacity were not verified.
The 2025 CCDR combines staff risk overlays and referenced studies of different vintages. Its co-location of climate impact and social exclusion does not establish a climate-caused conflict pathway.
A September 2026 peer-reviewed Boro/Okavango climate-conflict article was located, but its publisher full-text page returned 403. No claim was taken from the indexed abstract.
